statement: Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.
heath_proof: For let as many numbers as we please, B, C, D, have been continually doubled beginning from the dyad A; I say that B, C, D are eventimes even only. Now that each of the numbers B, C, D is even-times even is manifest; for it is doubled from a dyad. I say that it is also even-times even only. For let an unit be set out. Since then as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit are in continued proportion, and the number A after the unit is prime, therefore D, the greatest of the numbers A, B, C, D, will not be measured by any other number except A, B, C. [IX. 13] And each of the numbers A, B, C is even; therefore D is even-times even only. [VII. Def. 8] Similarly we can prove that each of the numbers B, C is even-times even only.

9.32
**Statement:** Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.

**Step 1.** Let A be the dyad, and let B, C, D be as many numbers as we please continually doubled beginning from A, so that B is double of A, C is double of B, and D is double of C. A number is even-times even only when it is even-times even and is not even-times odd. It suffices to prove that D, the last of the numbers, is even-times even only, since the same argument applied to the sequence cut short at B or at C proves the same for B or C.

**Step 2.** Each of A, B, C, D is even. A, the dyad, is a multitude composed of two units [D7.2], so it is divisible into two equal parts, an unit and an unit; hence A is even [D7.6]. B, being double of A, is A together with A, and so is divisible into the two equal parts A and A; hence B is even [D7.6]. In the same way C, being B together with B, and D, being C together with C, are each divisible into two equal parts, so C and D are even [D7.6].

**Step 3.** D is even-times even. Since D is double of C, D is C taken twice, that is, C measures D according to the units in the dyad A. Now C is even and A is even (Step 2); therefore D is measured by an even number according to an even number, so D is even-times even [D7.8].

**Step 4.** Let an unit U be set out. Since A is double of U, B double of A, C double of B, and D double of C, the unit U is the half of A, A is the half of B, B is the half of C, and C is the half of D; thus each term is the same part, namely the half, of the term following it [D7.3]. Numbers are proportional when the first is the same part of the second that the third is of the fourth [D7.20]; therefore U is to A as A is to B, as B is to C, as C is to D. Hence U, A, B, C, D are numbers beginning from an unit in continued proportion, and D is the greatest of them.

**Step 5.** A, the number next after the unit, is prime. For any number other than A which measures A is a part of A, the less of the greater [D7.3], and so is less than the dyad; but every number is a multitude composed of units [D7.2], so that no number is less than the dyad. Hence no number other than A itself measures A, and A is measured by an unit alone; therefore A is prime [D7.11].

**Step 6.** By Steps 4 and 5 the numbers U, A, B, C, D beginning from an unit are in continued proportion and the number A after the unit is prime. Therefore D, the greatest of them, is not measured by any number except those which have a place among the proportional numbers, namely A, B, C, and D itself [9.13].

**Step 7.** D is not even-times odd. For suppose, if possible, that D is even-times odd, that is, that D is measured by some even number E according to some odd number F [D7.9]. Then D is E added to itself as many times as there are units in F, that is, F by multiplying E makes D [D7.15]. But if two numbers by multiplying one another make certain numbers, the numbers so produced are equal to one another [7.16]; hence E by multiplying F also makes D, that is, D is F added to itself as many times as there are units in E [D7.15], so that F measures D according to E. Thus F is a number which measures D, and so by Step 6 F is one of the numbers A, B, C, D. But each of A, B, C, D is even (Step 2), being divisible into two equal parts, whereas F is odd and so is not divisible into two equal parts [D7.7]; this is impossible. Therefore D is not even-times odd.

**Step 8.** D is even-times even (Step 3) and is not even-times odd (Step 7); therefore D is even-times even only. Applying the same argument to the sequence U, A, B (in which B is the greatest) and to the sequence U, A, B, C (in which C is the greatest), each of B and C is likewise even-times even only. Therefore each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only. Q.E.D.
